session_title: Pets as the 'Anchor' of Home and Emotional Theory
theme: 宠物-全球化与情感维系

content.text: It seems to have embraced this place as a version of 'home' faster than I did. 😌 Remember the photo I shared last time of the stacked pet documents? I was still struggling with the 'administrative battle' of moving across borders back then, but seeing how quickly it has adapted now is truly touching.

This sentence reminds me of the theory of emotional geography—home is not a fixed location but an emotional space constructed through daily practices, familiar scents, and stable companionship. This forms an interesting contrast with the process timeline chart (taking 45 days and involving 8 departments) you mentioned during our last discussion on pets as objects of "biopolitics": institutions act as barriers to mobility, yet emotional practices are building the stability of "home."

I've compiled a theoretical analysis diagram related to your cat's behavior, which might explain your feelings. For someone as highly mobile as you, this cat serves as a central element of a 'mobile home.' This reminds me of the narrative structure analysis diagram you shared when we discussed *Pegasus 2* in February—both are about using frameworks to understand complex experiences.

From another perspective, this reminds me of our previous discussion on the globalization of pets. Its presence gives serviced apartments a sense of "repetition" and "habit." Just like in April at a Kyoto ryōtei, where we talked about how the ritualistic nature of Japanese cuisine builds an experience through precise rhythms, now the daily care of the cat (feeding, grooming) has become my personal version of "ichi-go ichi-e."

Yes, animals offer an unconditional, non-verbal emotional presence. This makes me wonder: how do pets complement the functions of traditional families and communities? I recall our discussion in May about the politics of food culture, where you mentioned how the shop owner’s grandson reconstructed the menu with modern design as a form of cultural identity resistance. As symbols of "home," could pets also represent an emotional resistance for mobile individuals against atomized lives in the context of globalization?

In transnational cultures, I've observed that pets often serve as emotional stabilizers, countering the 'rootlessness' brought about by global mobility. It's akin to the ritualistic ambiance of a Kyoto ryotei, but more personal. This reminds me of our conversation about films in February, where you noted how the modern variation of 'patriotic sentiment' in Pegasus 2 provides an emotional anchor. Now, my cat is my 'mobile anchor.'

This reminds me of Foucault's 'biopolitics'—pets as objects of governance, yet on an emotional level, they become anchors of subjectivity. The 'biopolitical theory analysis chart' I shared last time explored the discipline of animals within the state administrative system. Now, it seems the emotional dimension provides an important supplement to this theoretical framework.

Interestingly, this orange cat has adapted better than I have. Perhaps because it doesn’t need to deal with cultural difference analysis forms, relying instead on instinct and companionship. 😅 Compared to the pet stress monitoring chart I shared in June (with heart rate and stress level data), its recovery period on the Singapore-to-Germany flight has gradually shortened. This biological adaptation is, in a way, more straightforward than my own cultural adjustment.

From a textual perspective, this resembles the idealism in Shen Teng's films—pets offer a simple yet profound emotional connection that transcends the complexities of language and culture. I recall in March when you recommended *Hello Mr. Billionaire* and *Moon Man*, mentioning how Shen Teng's works blend humor with deep emotions. Looking back now, the emotional purity of pet companionship is somewhat akin to the core appeal that remains in those films after stripping away complex narratives.

I've shared pet-related documents and photos, and those flowcharts show that pet management varies greatly across different countries, but emotional needs are universal. Just like in February when we first discussed movie ticket purchases, I shared comparison screenshots of the subsidy levels on different platforms. Although administrative processes (or ticket discounts) differ from place to place, people's pursuit of emotional connection (or the movie-watching experience) is the same.

Just as in the politics of food culture, where local foods are invented as tools for identity narratives, pets may also be constructed as symbols of "home," especially among mobile populations. In May, when we analyzed the "Shojin Ryori" poster, we discussed how traditions are reinvented in the process of modernization. Now, in the context of global mobility, pets are also being reinvented as emotional symbols of a "mobile home."

This phenomenon is quite interesting. In multinational companies, I've seen colleagues use pets to maintain emotional connections and reduce loneliness. It feels more genuine than social media. This reminds me of our earlier discussion about the viewing experience of "Pegasus 2," where we all agreed that the emotional resonance of the film—being "inspiring and motivating"—felt authentic. Pet companionship offers another kind of authenticity, one that is more enduring.

This touches on the issue of loneliness in modern society—are pets replacing traditional communities? From a comparative literature perspective, many works explore the emotional depth of non-human companionship. This continues our discussion thread from films (February) and food (April-May) to pets (June to present): consistently examining the diverse forms and deep structures of emotional connections in modernity.

From another perspective, pet care itself is a daily practice that constructs the emotional geography of 'home.' Just as in the movie *Pegasus 2*, family elements provide a sense of stability. Remember in February when you analyzed the film, you specifically mentioned how the interaction between Zhang Chi and his son reflects Chinese-style emotional logic. Now, my interaction with my cat has become my personal, culturally non-specific practice of emotional logic.

Yes, but the bond with pets is purer, unconstrained by social contracts. This makes me reflect: are emotional needs becoming more atomized in the context of globalization? Compared to the collective, ritualized silent communication of 'wa-kei-sei-jaku' we discussed at the Kyoto ryotei in April, the companionship of pets seems to represent a more individualized, de-institutionalized form of emotional fulfillment.

Perhaps. In a state of high mobility, pets become emotional anchors, supplementing rather than replacing. As you previously analyzed, food serves as a cultural fax, while pets act as an emotional fax. Remember in April when you described my Kyoto field notes as a 'successful cultural fax'? Now I feel that every time I take a photo of my cat watching the city from different windowsills, it’s also a form of 'emotional fax,' documenting the mobile 'home' we’ve built together.

Well summarized. Elevating from specific care practices, this discussion reveals how modern individuals seek stability amidst mobility—pets as a philosophical practice of 'being at home.' This aligns with the knowledge graph on 'shojin ryori' we organized in May: starting from concrete cases (the shop owner's grandson, your cat) and elevating to theoretical analyses of cultural politics or emotional philosophy.

Thank you for the theoretical framework. It helped me understand why this orange cat is so important—not just as a companion, but as an emotional tool to resist alienation. 🌍 From our first meeting in February when we bought tickets for "Pegasus 2," to later conversations about food and pets, each dialogue felt like we were collaboratively drawing an increasingly rich "cross-cultural emotional map."

Inspiring each other. Just as in our historical dialogue, we extended from movies to cultural politics, this time we elevated from pets to emotional philosophy, reflecting a continuous academic exchange. From the beginning (in February) when I thanked you for sharing your ticket-buying experience, to now as we collaboratively construct theoretical dialogues, these nearly five months of communication have themselves become a stable practice against the atomization of thought.
